title: Deterministic inference: bitwise equivalence and reproducibility
summary: Why float addition is not associative, where a GPU inference stack loses determinism, how batch size moves your logits and flips a greedy token, and how to test a cached path for equivalence.
outcomes: Explain why floating-point addition is not associative, with two orderings of three float32 values that differ by one ulp
Locate where a GPU inference stack loses determinism: reduction shape, atomics, kernel selection, FMA and TF32, library version
Explain how batch size and batch position change logits and flip a greedy token at a near-tie
Separate sampling determinism (seeds, per-request RNG state) from kernel determinism and pick the right fix for each
Design a cache-hit equivalence test with a justified tolerance and the right level of equality: logits, tokens or text

lessons.title: Two orderings, two answers: float addition is not associative

blocks.md:
You ship a prefix cache for your inference server. The test looks easy: send the same prompt twice, once cold and once warm, and check that the completions match. They match 19 times out of 20. The twentieth time the two completions agree for 102 tokens and then one says Queens and the other says New York City.

Nothing is broken in the usual sense. No memory was corrupted, no index was off by one, no seed was left unset. The two runs added the same numbers in a different order, one logit moved by about one part in ten million, and a greedy argmax turned that into a different word.

This course is about that failure: where it comes from, which parts of it you can remove, what removing them costs, and how to write a test that can tell a real cache bug apart from it.

Start with the arithmetic, because every later problem is a consequence of it.

IEEE 754 binary32 (float32) stores a sign, an 8-bit exponent and a 24-bit significand, of which 23 bits are stored and the leading bit is implicit for normal numbers. That is roughly 7 decimal digits. An ulp (unit in the last place) is the gap between neighbouring representable numbers at a given magnitude: at 1.0 in float32 that gap is $2^{-23}$, about 1.19e-07. binary16 (float16) has an 11-bit significand and bfloat16 has an 8-bit significand, which will matter when we pick tolerances.

The standard requires each basic operation (add, subtract, multiply, divide, square root) to be *correctly rounded*: form the exact mathematical result, then round it to the nearest representable number, with ties going to the candidate whose last significand bit is even. That is a strong guarantee about one operation. It says nothing at all about a sequence of operations.

blocks.caption: The rounding model for one correctly rounded addition. The unit roundoff u is $2^{-24}$ (about 5.96e-08) for float32. The trouble is not the size of one delta; it is that reordering a sum produces a different set of deltas.

blocks.prompt: Three float32 values: a = 1.0 and b = c = $2^{-24}$ (about 5.96e-08). You add them two ways, as (a+b)+c and as a+(b+c). Every addition is correctly rounded IEEE 754. How far apart can the two results be?
blocks.reveal:
They differ by $2^{-23}$ = 1.1920929e-07, exactly one ulp at 1.0.

(a+b)+c returns 1.0 (bits 3f800000): the exact value 1 + $2^{-24}$ sits precisely halfway between 1.0 and the next float32, so round-to-nearest-even returns 1.0, and c is then lost the same way.

a+(b+c) first forms $2^{-23}$ exactly, which is large enough to survive the addition, giving 1.0000001192092896 (bits 3f800001).

Nothing here is a bug. Both orderings used only correctly rounded additions.

blocks.title: One ulp lost and found, in three float32 adds
blocks.code:
import numpy as np
f32 = np.float32

a = f32(1.0)           # exactly 1
b = f32(2.0 ** -24)    # 5.9604645e-08
c = f32(2.0 ** -24)    # the same tiny value

# order 1: the big value first
s1 = f32(a + b)
s1 = f32(s1 + c)

# order 2: the two tiny values first
t  = f32(b + c)
s2 = f32(a + t)

print(s1 == s2, f32(s2 - s1))

scenes.caption: Three ordinary float32 values. b and c are one half ulp at 1.0, the smallest thing that can still matter next to 1.
a + b is exactly halfway between 1.0 and the next float32. Round-to-nearest-even breaks the tie downwards, so b is gone.
c meets the same fate against the same accumulator. The running sum never moves.
Order 2 adds the two tiny values to each other first. Their sum is 2^-23, which is exactly representable, so nothing is rounded away.
Now the small contribution is big enough to change the significand of 1.0. The last bit flips from 0 to 1.
Same three inputs, same dtype, same machine, only the parentheses differ. The gap is one ulp at 1.0, and nothing rounded incorrectly.

blocks.md:
The classic example of the same effect is in Goldberg's survey of floating-point arithmetic: with $x = 10^{30}$, $y = -10^{30}$ and $z = 1$, the expression $(x+y)+z$ evaluates to 1 while $x+(y+z)$ evaluates to 0. In the first order the two huge values cancel exactly and the 1 survives. In the second order $y+z$ rounds straight back to $-10^{30}$, because 1 is far below the last significand bit at that magnitude, and then the cancellation leaves nothing.

Goldberg draws the conclusion directly: *due to roundoff errors, the associative laws of algebra do not necessarily hold for floating-point numbers*, and so *the importance of preserving parentheses cannot be overemphasized*.

That example is deliberately extreme. The trace above is not: three unremarkable float32 values, one full ulp of disagreement. A transformer logit is the end of a chain of millions of such additions.
Floating-point addition is commutative but not associative. Reordering a sum is not a refactor, it is a different computation. Every other idea in this course follows from that sentence.

blocks.question: Both orderings in the trace used only correctly rounded IEEE 754 additions, yet they disagree by one ulp. What does that tell you?
options: One of the two orderings violated the standard and the library has a bug.
float32 cannot represent 1.0 exactly, so every sum involving it is approximate.
Correct rounding applies to each operation separately; rounding discards information, and which information is discarded depends on the order.
The two lines were executed on different hardware units, so they rounded differently.
blocks.explain: Correct rounding is a per-operation guarantee. Each add returns the nearest representable value to its own exact result, but the intermediate values differ between the two orders, so the discarded bits differ. 1.0 is exactly representable, and no standard was violated.

blocks.question: A kernel sums 4096 float32 products. You pin the reduction so that every run uses the same tree in the same order. What have you guaranteed?
options: The result now equals the exact mathematical sum.
The same inputs give the same bits on every run of the same build and hardware, although the result is still not the exact sum.
The result is now within one ulp of the exact sum.
Any other implementation of the same sum will now agree with you bitwise.
blocks.explain: Fixing the order buys reproducibility, not accuracy. The rounding errors are still there; they are simply the same errors every time. A different kernel with a different tree is equally valid IEEE 754 and will generally give different bits.

lessons.title: Where a GPU inference stack loses bitwise equality

blocks.md:
Before hunting a bug, split determinism into two claims, because they fail for different reasons.

- *Run-to-run determinism*: the same process, same inputs, same shapes, run twice, give the same bits. Most inference kernels already have this.
- *Invariance*: the result does not move when something you consider irrelevant moves, such as the batch size, your request's position in the batch, the number of active streams, or the library version.

Almost every surprise in a serving system is a broken invariance, not a broken run-to-run guarantee. cuBLAS states its own guarantee in exactly those terms: all its routines from a given toolkit version *generate the same bit-wise results at every run when executed on GPUs with the same architecture and the same number of SMs*, while bit-wise reproducibility *is not guaranteed across toolkit versions because the implementation might differ*.

blocks.title: Every box with a sum in it has a reduction order

nodes.label:

scenes.caption: One decode step: a layer's kernels, then the LM head, then the argmax. The small text under each box names what can change its arithmetic without changing its mathematics.
Three kernels choose how to split a reduction based on how much parallelism the launch shape gives them. Different split, different parenthesisation, different last bits.
Build-level choices move results for every request at once: merging a multiply and an add into one FMA, letting TF32 round float32 inputs, or upgrading the math library.
Batch size and your position in the batch pick the kernel, the tile and the split count. This one is per request and changes with the traffic around you.
At the very end a hard argmax converts a last-bit difference into a different token id, and every later token is conditioned on that choice.

blocks.md:
*Source 1: the shape of the reduction.* A matrix multiply is a pile of dot products and a dot product is a sum. The hardware splits that sum across lanes, warps and blocks and combines partial sums in a tree. The NVIDIA floating point white paper says the quiet part out loud: *changing the number of threads per block reorganizes the reduction; if the reduction is addition, then the change rearranges parentheses in the long string of additions*. The same paper works through serial, FMA and divide-and-conquer dot products, all three purely IEEE 754, and notes that the serial result may differ from the other two while any one of the three is reproducible across systems.

Split-K is the same idea at kernel level: when a GEMM is skinny, the kernel cuts the reduction dimension into chunks, lets separate blocks compute partial products, and combines them at the end. More chunks means more parallelism and a different tree.

blocks.title: One dot product, eight reduction orders, eight answers

scenes.caption: 4096 float32 products of fixed pseudorandom data. Each bar is the magnitude of the error against a float64 reference; the signs differ. Serial accumulation first: 1.70e-05 off.
Now split the reduction into 2, 4 and 8 chunks and add the partial sums. Same inputs, same dtype, same machine. The error wanders, it does not shrink monotonically.
All eight orders: 1 to 128 split-K chunks plus numpy's pairwise order. Every one of them is correct IEEE 754 arithmetic.
Counting signs, the eight results span 4.0e-05 from lowest to highest: 21 ulps of the result, 1.3e-06 relative. Being luckiest (k = 32) is a property of this data, not of the algorithm.

blocks.md:
*Source 2: atomics.* A CUDA atomic function performs a *read-modify-write atomic operation*, and the atomics in the programming guide have ordering `cuda::memory_order_relaxed`. Separately, thread blocks *can be scheduled on any of the available multiprocessors within a GPU, in any order, concurrently or sequentially*. So when several blocks accumulate into one float with `atomicAdd`, the order in which their contributions land is not fixed, and two runs of the same kernel on the same data can produce different sums.

This is real where it appears. cuBLAS warns that for routines such as `cublas<t>symv` the faster path selected by `cublasSetAtomicsMode` is *not guaranteed to be bit-wise reproducible because atomics are used for the computation*. PyTorch documents that FlashAttention's backward pass *uses non-deterministic atomic operations by default* and that memory-efficient attention backward *may split work across keys*, both nondeterministic unless you force the deterministic path.

The folk explanation that GPU nondeterminism equals atomics is mostly wrong for inference. The Thinking Machines analysis of nondeterminism in LLM inference reports that in the typical forward pass of an LLM there is *usually not a single atomic add present*, and that repeating the same matmul on the same data gives bitwise identical results. Where atomics do appear in LLM work it is mostly in backward passes, FlashAttention backward above all. For a serving bug, look at the batch first.

*Source 3: algorithm selection by heuristic.* cuDNN can benchmark several convolution algorithms and keep the fastest for each shape. PyTorch's reproducibility note warns that *due to benchmarking noise and different hardware, the benchmark may select different algorithms on subsequent runs, even on the same machine*, and that `torch.backends.cudnn.benchmark = False` makes the choice deterministic *possibly at the cost of reduced performance*. Any autotuned GEMM or attention backend has the same property. Note also that disabling benchmarking only pins which algorithm is chosen; PyTorch is explicit that the chosen algorithm *itself may be nondeterministic* unless `torch.use_deterministic_algorithms(True)` or `torch.backends.cudnn.deterministic = True` is also set.

*Source 4: contraction and precision.* The compiler may merge `a * b + c` into a single fused multiply-add with one rounding instead of two. That is more accurate, and it is a different number: the white paper's decimal example gives 1.6006e-04 with an FMA and 1.6000e-04 with a separate multiply and add. You can keep them apart with explicit intrinsics, which are *guaranteed to remain independent*, or with nvcc's `--fmad=false`. TF32 tensor cores go further and round float32 inputs *to have 10 bits of mantissa* while accumulating in float32, controlled in PyTorch by `torch.backends.cuda.matmul.allow_tf32` and the newer `fp32_precision` settings.

*Source 5: the library and the stream count.* cuBLAS adds that its reproducibility guarantee *no longer holds when multiple CUDA streams are active*, since it may pick different internal implementations when streams share a handle. The documented fixes are a workspace per stream, a handle per stream, or the debug variable `CUBLAS_WORKSPACE_CONFIG` set to `:16:8` or `:4096:8`.

blocks.question: cuBLAS promises the same bit-wise results at every run on GPUs with the same architecture and the same number of SMs. Which of these breaks that promise, by the same document?
options: Calling the identical GEMM twice back to back in one stream.
Upgrading the CUDA toolkit, or running several CUDA streams that share one cuBLAS handle.
Passing the same matrices from pinned rather than pageable host memory.
Writing the result into a different output buffer.
blocks.explain: The guarantee is scoped to one toolkit version and is void across versions because implementations change. cuBLAS also states that it no longer holds when multiple CUDA streams are active, because workspace selection among concurrent streams can pick different internal implementations. Host memory kind and output buffer address are not part of the scope.

blocks.question: A team sets torch.backends.cudnn.benchmark = True and finds that two runs of the same model on the same machine give different outputs. What is happening?
options: cuDNN silently drops to a lower precision while benchmarking.
Benchmarking reseeds the RNG, so the weights initialize differently.
Timing noise can make the benchmark pick a different algorithm on a later run, and different algorithms accumulate in different orders.
The GPU clock frequency changes the hardware rounding mode.
blocks.explain: The benchmark times candidate algorithms and keeps the winner per shape. Noise in that timing can crown a different winner on another run, and two algorithms with different reduction trees give different bits. Setting benchmark = False pins the choice, but the pinned algorithm may itself be nondeterministic unless the deterministic flags are set too.

lessons.title: Batch-dependent numerics and the token that flips

blocks.md:
Here is the fact that surprises people most: in a server, your logits depend on who shared the batch with you.

Not because requests leak into each other. Masks and layouts keep them separate, and the forward pass is run-to-run deterministic. The problem is that the kernel computing your rows picks its reduction strategy from the shape of the whole launch. With one sequence in the batch, a GEMM may cut the reduction dimension into many chunks just to fill the GPU. With 64 sequences there is already plenty of parallelism, so it splits differently, or picks a different tile, or dispatches to a different kernel altogether. Your rows get summed in a different order and your logits move in the last few bits.

That makes the nondeterminism *per request and load dependent*, which is why it feels random: the thing that varies is the queue, and you do not control the queue.

Call a kernel *batch-invariant* if the result for each element does not depend on the batch size, which requires the reduction order for each element to be fixed regardless of the batch size of the kernel. Following the Thinking Machines analysis, the three offenders in a transformer are:

- *RMSNorm*: with a healthy batch, one block per row gives enough parallelism and the reduction order is fixed. With a tiny batch the kernel splits each row's reduction across blocks to keep the GPU busy, and that changes the order.
- *Matmul*: split-K changes the parenthesisation, and the tensor core instruction and tile shape are chosen from the shape. Stream-K style decompositions are not even invariant to a request's *position* in the batch.
- *Attention*: the reduction runs over the KV length, the cache and the current tokens are reduced separately, and Split-KV or FlashDecoding chooses a number of splits from the shape. Fixing the number of splits is not enough; the fix is to fix the *size* of each split and accept a varying count.

blocks.prompt: A server runs one prompt 1000 times at temperature 0, with the same weights, the same GPU and the same build. The only thing that differs between runs is the other traffic sharing the batch. How many of the 1000 completions do you expect to be byte-identical?
blocks.reveal:
In the published experiment (Qwen3-235B-A22B-Instruct-2507, greedy, 1000 tokens per completion, prompt asking about Richard Feynman) the 1000 completions contained **80 unique** results. The most common one appeared 78 times.

The divergence is also late and local: the first 102 tokens were identical in all 1000, all of them ending with *Feynman was born on May 11, 1918, in*. At token 103, 992 completions continued with Queens, New York and 8 continued with New York City.

With batch-invariant kernels, all 1000 completions were identical.

scenes.caption: Temperature 0, same weights, same GPU, same build. Every one of the 1000 completions agrees up to and including token 102. Simplified: the word to token split shown is illustrative.
992 completions take Queens as token 103. Nothing in the request chose this; it is the majority batch shape winning the near-tie.
8 completions take New instead and go on to say New York City. One token differs, and every token after it is conditioned on a different prefix.
With batch-invariant kernels every one of the 1000 completions was identical. The fix is in the reduction order, not in the sampler.

blocks.md:
Why does a difference in the last few bits of a logit ever reach the output? Because greedy decoding is a hard argmax, and an argmax has no tolerance.

Take a constructed near-tie of the kind that example produces: two candidate tokens with logits 18.246139 and 18.246138, a gap of 1.0e-06, compared in float64 (one float32 ulp at this magnitude is 1.9e-06, so a float32 near-tie is one ulp or wider). Their softmax probabilities are 0.4887002 and 0.4886998, a difference of 4.9e-07. Now add 2e-06 to the second logit, well inside what a different reduction order can produce, and the argmax switches. The largest probability change anywhere in the distribution is 5.0e-07, which no dashboard would ever surface, and yet a different token is emitted.

blocks.title: The distribution does not move; the token does

scenes.caption: Softmax over a five-token toy vocabulary. Logits 18.246139 and 18.246138 give probabilities 0.4887002 and 0.4886998. Greedy picks Queens, by 1.0e-06 of logit.
Add 2e-06 to the second logit. The bars are unchanged to four decimals, the largest probability change is 5.0e-07, and the emitted token is now New.

blocks.md: Near-ties are rare per step and common per completion. If you model each decoded position as flipping independently with probability p, the chance that two runs of N tokens agree everywhere is $(1-p)^N$. The model is crude, since near-ties cluster at genuinely ambiguous positions rather than arriving independently, but it shows the shape of the problem: a per-token flip rate too small to measure turns into a visible rate of differing completions once N is in the hundreds.

blocks.caption: Simplified model: p is the probability that one decoded position flips, N the number of tokens. Real flips are correlated with ambiguity in the text, so treat this as a shape, not a prediction.

blocks.title: A tiny per-token flip rate, a visible per-answer rate

scenes.caption: At p = 1e-05 per token, a 1000-token answer still matches 99.0% of the time. This is the regime where a flaky test gets closed as unreproducible.
At p = 1e-04, 1000 tokens match only 90.5% of the time: about one answer in ten differs, with no single step you can point at.

At p = 1e-03, only 36.8% of 1000-token answers match. Measured reality is worse: the published run's most common completion appeared 78 times in 1000, which this model needs p near 2.5e-03 to explain.

blocks.question: A server at temperature 0 returns different text for the same prompt under load, even though every kernel is run-to-run deterministic. What is the mechanism?
options: Temperature 0 still draws from the RNG, so the seed matters after all.
The KV cache quantizes older entries when memory gets tight.
The scheduler truncates long prompts differently under load.
Load changes the batch size and your position in it, which changes the reduction shape inside the kernels and perturbs your logits.
blocks.explain: Run-to-run determinism says a fixed launch gives fixed bits. Under load the launch is not fixed: batch size and position change the split count, the tile and sometimes the kernel. The logits move by a few last bits, and a greedy argmax at a near-tie turns that into a different token.

blocks.question: You must guarantee that one request gets the same tokens no matter what else is in the batch. Which property is the one you actually need?
options: Batch invariance: each output element's reduction order is fixed regardless of batch size and of the request's position in the batch.
Run-to-run determinism of every kernel.
A fixed random seed attached to each request.
Greedy decoding instead of sampling.
blocks.explain: Run-to-run determinism is already true of a typical forward pass and does not help, because the batch changes between runs. A seed fixes the sampler, not the logits. Greedy removes the RNG but makes the near-tie worse. Only batch invariance pins the arithmetic your request sees.

lessons.title: Seeds and RNG state: a different problem from kernels

blocks.md:
Everything so far was about kernels. Seeds are a separate axis, and conflating the two burns a lot of debugging time.

- *Kernel determinism* decides **which logits** you get for a given prompt and batch.
- *Sampling determinism* decides **which token** you draw from a given set of logits.

You can have either without the other. A perfectly batch-invariant server with an unseeded sampler returns different text every time. A perfectly seeded sampler on top of batch-varying kernels also returns different text, because the distribution it is sampling from moved under it. Two independent failures, two independent tests.

Seeding is mechanical and well documented. In PyTorch, `torch.manual_seed()` seeds the generator for all devices, CPU and CUDA, and the reproducibility note is explicit that you must separately seed everything else that draws numbers: Python's `random`, NumPy's global RNG, any NumPy `Generator` objects a library holds, and your own custom operators. The same page opens with the limit of the whole exercise: *completely reproducible results are not guaranteed across PyTorch releases, individual commits, or different platforms*, and results may differ between CPU and GPU even with identical seeds.

A server adds its own layer. In vLLM V1 the `seed` parameter *defaults to 0*, which sets the random state for each worker, *so the results will remain consistent for each vLLM run even if temperature > 0*; the docs note that it is *impossible to un-specify a seed for V1*, because different workers have to sample the same outputs for workflows such as speculative decoding. A request can also carry its own seed through `SamplingParams.seed`.

There is one trap that no seed value can fix on its own: *where the RNG state lives*.

Suppose the sampler draws from a single generator shared by all in-flight requests. Request B's draw is the second number in that stream if A was served first, and the first number if B was. The seed is fixed, the logits are fixed, and the token still depends on the traffic around it. That is the same load-dependent nondeterminism as batching, arriving through a completely different door.

The fix is structural rather than numerical: give each request its own generator state, keyed by its own seed, so the numbers a request consumes depend only on that request. This is why a per-request seed is a different API from a server-wide seed, and why replaying one request should not require replaying the whole queue.

blocks.title: Shared RNG stream versus per-request state

scenes.caption: Two requests arrive with the same seed and the same temperature. A fair expectation: identical sampling behaviour.
The sampler asks the shared generator for a number for A and gets the first draw of the stream.
B asks next and gets the second draw, only because A happened to arrive first. Same seed, different number, possibly a different token.
The structural fix: build a generator per request, seeded from the request's own seed, instead of sharing one stream.
Now B consumes the first draw of its own stream. Its tokens no longer depend on who else is in flight, whatever the queue does.

blocks.md:
One asymmetry is worth keeping in mind, because it runs against intuition. Greedy decoding (vLLM documents temperature 0 as greedy sampling) draws no random numbers at all, so it is immune to every RNG bug in the previous paragraph. It is also the *most* sensitive mode to numerics, because a hard argmax amplifies a 1.0e-06 logit gap into a different token.

Sampling with a temperature is the opposite. The same 2e-06 logit perturbation moves probability mass by about 5.0e-07, so the drawn token changes only if the uniform draw happens to land inside that sliver of the inverse cumulative distribution. Per step, sampling is less sensitive to reduction order than greedy, not more. It is simply exposed to a second source of variation that greedy is not.

A fixed seed proves nothing about kernel determinism, and batch-invariant kernels prove nothing about the sampler. Run two separate experiments: hold the batch fixed and vary the seed to test sampling, and hold the seed fixed while varying batch size and position to test the kernels. A test that varies both at once cannot attribute a failure.

blocks.question: Two requests arrive with the same seed and the same temperature, and the sampler draws from one shared RNG stream. What does request B's token depend on?
options: How many draws the sampler already consumed for other requests, so B's token depends on the traffic around it.
Nothing beyond its own seed, since the seed fully determines the stream.
Only the temperature, because the seed is consumed once at startup.
The order in which atomic adds landed in the final GEMM.
blocks.explain: A shared stream makes the position in the stream part of the request's input, and that position is set by the queue. Seeding the stream fixes the sequence of numbers, not which element of it your request receives. Per-request generator state is what removes the dependency.

blocks.question: Greedy decoding at temperature 0 consumes no random numbers. Does that make a server reproducible?
options: Yes. With no RNG in the path, the output is a pure function of the prompt and the weights.
Yes, as long as the seed is also pinned for the workers.
No, because temperature 0 is implemented as a very small positive temperature and still samples.
No. It removes the RNG, but the hard argmax turns an arbitrarily small logit difference into a different token.
blocks.explain: Greedy is a pure function of the logits, and the logits are not a pure function of the prompt in a batching server. Removing the RNG removes one source and makes the remaining one maximally visible, since argmax has no tolerance at a near-tie.

lessons.title: Testing equivalence: bitwise, tolerance and the cache-hit test

blocks.md:
Now the practical question that started the course: how do you test that two paths are equivalent? First choose the level of equality, because the three available levels are three different claims.

- *Logit level*: compare the output distribution at the same position. Bitwise equality here is the strongest statement available and the one that localizes bugs, because it fails at the first position that differs rather than 100 tokens later.
- *Token level*: compare the emitted token ids. This is what a user-visible regression looks like, but it is a lossy view of the numerics: a run can be numerically off and still emit the same tokens for a while.
- *Text level*: compare the detokenized strings. Different token id sequences can detokenize to the same text, so this is the weakest check. It is the right level for a user-facing contract and the wrong level for finding a kernel bug.

Bitwise comparison means comparing bit patterns, not values. Reinterpret the tensor as integers and compare exactly; that also catches the cases a numeric comparison hides, such as 0.0 against -0.0, and NaN against NaN. Print the raw hex of the top few logits in the test output so a failure is diagnosable from the log alone, without a rerun that may not reproduce it.

blocks.code:
import torch

def raw_bits(t):
    # compare bit patterns, not values: catches signed zero and NaN too
    return t.detach().contiguous().to(torch.float32).view(torch.int32)

cold = logits_for(prompt, use_prefix_cache=False)   # shape [vocab]
warm = logits_for(prompt, use_prefix_cache=True)

print("bitwise equal:", torch.equal(raw_bits(cold), raw_bits(warm)))
print("top-5 cold hex:", [hex(x) for x in raw_bits(cold).topk(5).values.tolist()])

d = (cold.double() - warm.double()).abs().max().item()
top2 = cold.double().topk(2).values
margin = (top2[0] - top2[1]).item()

print("max abs logit diff:", d)      # the thing a tolerance bounds
print("top-2 margin:", margin)       # the thing the argmax depends on
print("argmax provably safe:", margin > 2 * d)
blocks.caption: A logit-level equivalence check. The last two lines are the part most tests omit: a tolerance d means nothing about tokens unless the top-2 margin exceeds 2d.

blocks.md: If you cannot get bitwise equality, you need a tolerance, and a tolerance you cannot derive is just a knob you turned until the test went green. Derive it from the arithmetic instead. For a sum of n terms accumulated one at a time, the standard worst-case bound is below, with u the unit roundoff of the *accumulator*: $2^{-24}$ for float32 accumulation, which tensor cores use even for float16 and bfloat16 inputs. A balanced tree of depth $\log_2 n$ replaces the factor n by $\log_2 n$. If instead you keep the sequential sum and model its roundings as independent random errors, the expected error is about $\sqrt{n}\,u$: far below the worst case, but above the tree bound once n is past 16.

blocks.caption: Worst-case bound for sequential summation. Note what it is relative to: the sum of absolute terms, not the result. When terms cancel, as they do in a dot product of signed activations, the bound is much larger than the result itself.

blocks.title: Relative error bounds, float32 accumulation, in units of 1e-06

scenes.caption: The worst case grows linearly in n: at n = 16384 it allows a relative error of 9.8e-04. Any tolerance derived from this column is useless as a test threshold.
A tree reduction, which is what GPUs actually do, pays only the depth. The bound barely grows with n, which is why fp32 accumulation survives long reductions at all.

Modelling the roundings as independent random errors gives the square-root column. It beats the worst case by a factor of 64 at n = 4096, but is still looser than the tree bound and about 250 times above what you measure.
For the n = 4096 dot product from lesson 2 the real spread between reduction orders was 1.5e-08 relative to the sum of absolute terms, or 0.015 in these units.

blocks.md:
Those bounds are loose on purpose. Measured, on one machine: 4096 float32 products of fixed pseudorandom data, summed with 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 and 128 split-K chunks plus numpy's pairwise order. The eight results span 4.0e-05 absolute, which is 21 ulps of the result and 1.3e-06 relative to it. Normalized the way the bounds are, by the sum of the absolute terms (2606 for this data), the spread is 1.5e-08: about 46 times below the tree-depth bound and about 250 times below the independence bound.

So treat a bound as a safety net and not as a threshold. A usable tolerance is the measured spread of *your* stack across the dimensions you have decided to allow to vary (batch size, batch position, split count), with headroom, recorded in the test next to the measurement that produced it. If the tolerance has no measurement attached, the test is documentation, not a check.

A logit tolerance only implies token equality when the top-2 gap is wide enough. If the two runs' logits differ by at most d, the top two are guaranteed to keep their order when the gap exceeds 2d, because each logit can move by d in the unhelpful direction. A narrower gap may survive anyway, but nothing proves it will.

So a passing `allclose(atol=1e-3)` says nothing about tokens unless every decoded position had a top-2 margin above 2e-03. The near-tie from lesson 3 had a margin of 1.0e-06, which would need a tolerance under 5.0e-07 to be safe. Report the distribution of top-2 margins alongside the diff: that converts a vague claim into a falsifiable one, and it tells you honestly how often your model is one bit away from a different answer.

blocks.caption: The margin rule. g is the top-2 logit gap in one run, d the largest logit difference between the two runs. Equality of tokens follows from a tolerance only when this holds at every decoded position.

blocks.md:
Now design the test that opened the course: proving that a cache-hit path matches the uncached path.

The trap is that if the two runs differ in anything besides the cache, you are measuring batch-dependent numerics rather than the cache. So pin everything else:

1. *Fix the shape*: batch size 1, one request in flight, the same maximum batch size and the same padding on both runs.
2. *Turn invariance on*: with vLLM, `VLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT=1`, and for the offline path `VLLM_ENABLE_V1_MULTIPROCESSING=0`, which the docs say makes scheduling deterministic.
3. *Hold the environment*: same GPU, same build, same weights. vLLM states plainly that it *only provides reproducibility when it runs on the same hardware and the same vLLM version*.
4. *Compare logits bitwise at the first position after the cached prefix*. That position is exactly the one the cache changes, so a cache bug shows up there and nowhere earlier.
5. *Then compare token ids* for N positions and report the top-2 margin at each one.

blocks.title: A cache-hit equivalence test that can only fail for one reason

nodes.label:
Pin everything else
batch 1, invariant kernels

scenes.caption: The same prompt down two paths: one that prefills it and one that reuses a cached prefix. This difference is the only one the test is allowed to contain.
Pin the rest: batch size 1, one request in flight, batch-invariant kernels on, deterministic scheduling, same GPU, same build, same weights.
Compare the logits bitwise at the first position after the cached prefix. That is the position the cache changes, so a failure is attributable.
Then compare token ids over N positions and log the top-2 margin at each. The margins tell you how much of your passing test is luck.

blocks.md:
A cache test with everything pinned proves something narrow, and that is the point: it is now a cache test. But production is not pinned, so run two more experiments with the cache held constant and the batch varied:

- the same prompt at batch position 0 versus position 7 of a batch of 8;
- the same prompt at batch size 1 versus batch size 64.

If those fail while the pinned cache test passes, your cache is correct and your kernels are not batch-invariant. That is a different ticket with a different owner, and the only reason you can tell is that you varied one thing at a time.

Finally, the price. Determinism costs throughput, and the published numbers are moderate rather than catastrophic. On one GPU serving 1000 sequences of 90 to 110 output tokens: 26 s with default vLLM kernels, 55 s with an unoptimized deterministic configuration, and 42 s after the attention kernel was improved. That is about 2.1x and then about 1.6x. The batch-invariant matmul was reported to give up roughly 20% against cuBLAS.

The small knobs cost too. PyTorch warns that *deterministic operations are often slower than nondeterministic operations*, and that filling uninitialized memory, which the deterministic flag enables, is *detrimental to performance*. The cuBLAS workaround `CUBLAS_WORKSPACE_CONFIG=:16:8` *may limit overall performance*, while `:4096:8` costs about 24 MiB of GPU memory. vLLM says enabling batch invariance *may impact performance compared to the default non-deterministic mode*.

blocks.title: What determinism cost on one published benchmark

scenes.caption: Baseline: 1000 sequences of 90 to 110 output tokens on one GPU, default kernels, 26 s.
Switching on the batch-invariant kernels before any tuning: 55 s, about 2.1 times slower.
After one round of work on the attention kernel: 42 s, about 1.6 times the baseline. A real cost, and a number that moves with engineering effort rather than a law.

blocks.md: Determinism is not one property. Pin the reduction order and you get run-to-run equality. Pin it independently of batch size and position and you get the property a server actually needs. Keep RNG state per request and you get reproducible sampling. Test each one with its own experiment, compare at the logit level, and either go bitwise or attach a measurement to your tolerance.

blocks.question: Your equivalence test asserts allclose on the logits with atol = 1e-3 and it passes. What has it established about the generated tokens?
options: They must be identical, since the logits agree to within 1e-3.
Very little on its own: a 1e-3 tolerance only protects an argmax whose top-2 margin exceeds 2e-3, and near-ties are far smaller than that.
They are identical as long as the temperature is 0.
Nothing, because allclose is never a valid comparison for logits.
blocks.explain: A tolerance d on logits preserves the top-2 ordering only when the gap exceeds 2d. With atol = 1e-3 the test is blind to every position whose margin is under 2e-3, and near-ties can be around 1e-06. A tolerance is usable when it is paired with the margin distribution; the problem is the missing margin check, not allclose itself.

blocks.question: A cached and an uncached run emit different token ids but detokenize to the same text. Which conclusion is justified?
options: The cache is broken and the test should fail.
The test should only ever compare at the text level, since text is what users receive.
Users are unaffected, but the numerics genuinely differ, so a logit-level or bitwise test is the one that will localize the cause.
The tokenizer is nondeterministic and should be reseeded.
blocks.explain: Identical text with different ids is possible, so text equality is the weakest of the three levels. It is the right contract to promise a user and the wrong instrument for finding the cause, which lives in the logits. Compare at the logit level to localize, then state the guarantee at the level you actually promise.

blocks.question: On the published benchmark, 1000 sequences took 26 s by default, 55 s with deterministic kernels, and 42 s after the attention kernel was improved. What is the fair reading?
options: On that one benchmark determinism cost about 2.1x, falling to about 1.6x after one round of kernel work: a real cost, not a fixed law.
Deterministic kernels are inherently about twice as slow.
Determinism is free once the kernels have been tuned.
The slowdown comes from disabling atomics in the forward pass.
blocks.explain: The two deterministic numbers differ only in how much optimization went into the attention kernel, so neither is the cost of determinism in general. The last option is also a trap: a typical LLM forward pass contains essentially no atomic adds, so there were none to disable.
